domains.name: Biotech and Longevity

scenarios.title: Draw the Line
scenarios.situation: A clinic offers 'CRISPR enhancement' for healthy clients — unapproved, offshore, expensive.
choices: Red-flag cluster: germline-adjacent enhancement, no regulatory oversight, no off-target verification, wealthy-client targeting — this is the unethical frontier; the bright lines (somatic therapy vs enhancement, approved vs experimental) exist for reasons written in past tragedies
Medical tourism is fine — personal choice
It's the future — get in early
Only the price is objectionable
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The ethical framework here is settled among serious practitioners: somatic therapy for disease (regulated, verified) vs enhancement (uncontrolled, heritable risks). Offshore unapproved editing combines every red flag — no verification, no oversight, no recourse. 'Personal choice' doesn't cover germline consequences.
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes therapy from enhancement — and who verifies safety?

scenarios.title: Grade the Claim
scenarios.situation: A supplement claims 'reverses aging' citing a mouse study and 50 testimonials.
scenarios.prompt: What evidence tier is this, and what's missing?
choices: Tier 4 (anecdote) + misused Tier 2: mouse data doesn't transfer directly, testimonials aren't data — missing: human RCTs, biomarker validation, independent replication; the claim outruns the evidence by three tiers
Convincing — 50 testimonials!
Mouse studies prove human efficacy
All supplements are scams — dismiss
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Evidence tiers discipline the assessment: testimonials are Tier 4 (worthless for efficacy), mouse data is Tier 2 (suggestive, not dispositive). 'Reverses aging' in humans needs human RCTs — the claim leaps three tiers. Neither credulity nor blanket dismissal is analytical.
scenarios.hint: What would move this claim up one tier — and then another?

scenarios.title: Govern the Dual Use
scenarios.situation: Your foundry can synthesize arbitrary DNA. A customer orders a sequence of concern.
choices: Refuse and report: synthesis screening for sequences of concern is the industry's biosecurity duty — the dual-use dilemma is resolved by refusal plus reporting, not by 'customer privacy'; know the screening lists and the reporting channels
Fulfill it — customer is king
Fulfill but keep records
Ignore — it's probably fine
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Biosecurity is non-negotiable infrastructure: screening and refusal for sequences of concern, with reporting to appropriate channels. 'Customer privacy' doesn't cover bioweapon precursors. The field's social license depends on this discipline.
scenarios.hint: What is the foundry's duty when the order matches a concern list?

scenarios.title: Thesis the Biotech
scenarios.situation: A biotech pitches: novel mechanism, mouse data, $500M valuation, Phase 1 in 3 years.
choices: Five-question frame: mechanism plausibility + evidence tier (mouse = early), regulatory path length (Phase 1 in 3 years is optimistic), market/reimbursement reality, team track record, and IP moat — then price the risk: most such pitches fail; the valuation must reflect the attrition odds
Invest — novel mechanisms win
Pass — biotech is too hard
Invest small — FOMO hedge
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Biotech investing is attrition math: ~90% of preclinical assets fail. The five-question frame (science, regulatory, market, team, moat) plus honest timeline assessment prices the risk. Mouse-data valuations at $500M need extraordinary justification — the base rate is failure.
scenarios.hint: What is the base rate for preclinical assets — and what justifies beating it?

scenarios.title: Measure the Loop
scenarios.situation: Two synbio foundries: A publishes breakthroughs; B publishes cycle-time improvements. Which is the better bet?
scenarios.prompt: What does the DBTL lens say?
choices: B, usually: DBTL cycle time is the field's Moore's law — faster iteration compounds into more breakthroughs; breakthrough announcements are lagging indicators of past cycle speed, while cycle-time improvements predict future breakthrough rate
A — breakthroughs are what matter
Neither — synbio is hype
Both equally
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Iteration speed predicts discovery rate: the foundry compressing design-build-test-learn cycles will out-discover the one celebrating past wins. Breakthroughs are outputs; cycle time is the input. Bet on the input.
scenarios.hint: What produces breakthroughs — and which foundry is improving it?

domains.summary: CRISPR, synthetic biology, and the longevity frontier — biology becomes engineering.

domains.name: Space and Robotics

scenarios.title: Bet on the Curve
scenarios.situation: A space startup's business needs $500/kg launch. Current price: $3k/kg. They're launching now.
choices: Curve-dependent and premature: the business case requires a 6× cost reduction that may take a decade — launching now burns capital waiting for the curve; the disciplined play is timing entry to curve milestones, not hoping the curve hurries
Launch now — first mover advantage
The curve will hurry because they're launching
Pivot to something needing $3k/kg
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. $/kg-gated businesses must time entry to the cost curve — launching 6× too early means burning runway while waiting for physics and manufacturing to catch up. Hope isn't a strategy; milestone-timed entry is. Pivoting to fit current prices is the alternative honest answer.
scenarios.hint: What has to be true about launch costs — and when will it be?

scenarios.title: Demand Deployment Data
scenarios.situation: A humanoid robotics company shows an amazing demo video and seeks a factory pilot. No deployment data shared.
scenarios.prompt: What do you require before the pilot?
choices: Deployment metrics: interventions per hour, task completion rate in uncurated environments, MTBF — demos are marketing; the pilot decision needs operational data from real (not staged) operation
The video is enough — impressive!
Pilot immediately — first mover
Reject — humanoids are hype
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The demo-to-deployment gap is where robotics companies die: curated videos hide edge-case failures. Interventions-per-hour and uncurated task completion are the honest metrics. Pilots without them are expensive experiments disguised as decisions.
scenarios.hint: What happens in hour 8 of an uncut shift — not in the 2-minute video?

scenarios.title: Sequence the Resources
scenarios.situation: A lunar venture wants to mine helium-3 first, skipping water ice.
choices: Wrong keystone: water ice → propellant depots enable everything else (including He-3 transport economics); skipping the foundation resource for the exotic one inverts the dependency chain — propellant infrastructure comes first
He-3 is more valuable — correct priority
Do both simultaneously
Lunar mining is impossible anyway
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Resource strategy follows dependency chains: propellant from lunar water unlocks the cis-lunar economy that makes everything else (including He-3) transportable. Starting with the exotic resource skips the infrastructure it depends on. Keystone first.
scenarios.hint: What has to exist before He-3 can be economically transported?

scenarios.title: Respect the Regime
scenarios.situation: Your space startup wants to hire foreign engineers for propulsion work and share designs with an overseas partner.
choices: ITAR/EAR: rocket propulsion is munitions-adjacent — deemed exports (sharing with foreign nationals, even domestically) and physical exports need licenses; violations carry personal criminal liability — compliance isn't optional or deferrable
It's fine — engineers are engineers
Just don't tell anyone
Incorporate offshore to avoid it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. ITAR/EAR control space technology as defense articles: deemed exports to foreign nationals (even in the US office) require authorization, with personal criminal liability for violations. 'Offshore incorporation' to evade is itself a violation pattern. Compliance is day-one infrastructure.
scenarios.hint: What does 'deemed export' mean for your hiring plan?

scenarios.title: Decide Deliberately
scenarios.situation: You're offered a role building satellite systems with clear military applications. The pay is excellent.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right way to decide?
choices: Deliberate dual-use policy: research the actual applications, consult the ethical frameworks that matter to you, talk to practitioners on both sides — then decide consciously; drift (accepting without thought) and reflex (rejecting without thought) are both failures of agency
Take it — pay is pay
Reject it — all military work is wrong
Decide based on what friends think
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Dual-use careers deserve deliberate ethics: informed by actual applications (not abstractions), tested against your real values, decided consciously. Both unthinking acceptance and unthinking refusal abdicate the judgment that makes the decision yours.
scenarios.hint: What will you have built in 10 years — and can you stand behind it?

domains.summary: Reusable rockets, autonomous systems, and the economics of the space frontier.

domains.name: Fusion Energy

scenarios.title: Choose the Confinement Path
scenarios.situation: A new fusion venture must commit to magnetic confinement (tokamak/stellarator) or inertial confinement (laser-driven implosion). The founders ask which is 'the right' approach.
choices: Magnetic: tokamaks are the only serious path
Inertial: lasers are the future

Neither is 'the right' path in the abstract: the choice depends on the venture's theory of advantage — magnetic confinement has the deepest physics database and the ITER-scale validation path; inertial has NIF's ignition demonstration and different engineering challenges — evaluate against capital, timeline, and team, not ideology
Both simultaneously: hedge by building both
scenarios.why: Confinement choice is strategy, not theology: magnetic confinement offers decades of plasma-physics data and a clear (if slow) validation ladder, while inertial confinement has demonstrated ignition and faces different engineering scaling problems. The right choice depends on the venture's capital depth, timeline tolerance, and team expertise. Building both halves every resource and doubles every problem.
scenarios.hint: What does each path offer that the other does not?
objectives: Match path to capital, timeline, and team

scenarios.title: Reading the Q Announcement
scenarios.situation: A startup announces 'Q > 1' — more fusion energy out than heating energy in. Headlines declare the energy problem solved.
scenarios.prompt: What questions does the hype-cycle checklist demand before celebrating?
choices: None: Q > 1 is the milestone; the rest is engineering

Which Q: scientific Q (fusion power vs heating power) or engineering Q (electricity out vs electricity in)? Was it sustained or a millisecond pulse? What is the path from this plasma result to a power plant — materials, tritium supply, maintenance — and who verified the numbers?
What is the stock price: that is the real metric
How soon can I buy the home reactor: that is what matters
scenarios.why: Q has definitions, and the definition is the story: scientific breakeven (a plasma milestone, achieved) is orders of magnitude from engineering breakeven (a power plant). Duration, reproducibility, independent verification, and the named blockers between plasma and grid — tritium breeding, materials surviving neutron flux, maintainability — are what the signal checklist requires. Headlines report the number; the strategist reads the definition.
scenarios.hint: What is the distance from this Q to electricity on the grid?
objectives: Distinguish scientific Q from engineering Q
evidence: Which Q? How long? Verified by whom? Then what?

scenarios.title: The Tritium Problem
scenarios.situation: Your fusion plant design assumes deuterium-tritium fuel. A reviewer flags tritium supply: tritium is rare, radioactive with a 12-year half-life, and current global inventory is kilograms.
scenarios.prompt: How does a serious design answer this?
choices: Ignore it: fuel supply is a detail for later

With the tritium breeding blanket: the design must breed its own tritium from lithium in the reactor blanket — breeding ratio above 1 is a core design requirement, not an accessory, and the blanket is among the hardest engineering in the plant
Switch to fossil fuels as backup
Assume governments will supply tritium indefinitely
scenarios.why: D-T fusion eats tritium and the world has almost none — so every serious D-T plant design breeds its own via lithium blankets, and the tritium breeding ratio is a pass/fail design parameter. This is the materials-and-fuel lesson made concrete: the fuel cycle is not a detail, it is the plant. Designs that hand-wave breeding are not designs.
scenarios.hint: Where does a D-T plant's tritium come from?
objectives: Design tritium breeding as core requirement

scenarios.title: Materials Under Neutron Flux
scenarios.situation: The plasma physics of your design is excellent. The materials team reports that no available structural material survives the expected 14 MeV neutron flux for the plant's planned maintenance interval.
choices: Overrule them: plasma physics is the hard part and it is solved

Treat materials as the critical path: fusion's hardest unsolved problems are materials and engineering, not plasma — redirect resources to materials qualification, blanket design, and maintenance strategy, because a plant that cannot survive its own neutrons is not a plant
Extend the maintenance interval on paper to make the numbers work
Switch to a fuel with no neutrons and restart the physics
scenarios.why: This is the classic fusion mis-prioritization: the plasma is the celebrated problem, but materials under neutron bombardment are the binding constraint on every D-T design. Aneutronic fuels are a research topic, not a pivot. Paper extensions of maintenance intervals are fraud-adjacent. The plant lives or dies on materials — fund accordingly.
scenarios.hint: What kills a D-T plant faster: plasma instability or wall failure?
objectives: Prioritize materials as the critical path
evidence: A plant that cannot survive its neutrons is not a plant

scenarios.title: The Timeline Question
scenarios.situation: An investor asks when fusion will meaningfully contribute to the grid: 2030s, 2040s, or 'never in my lifetime'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest, useful answer?
choices: 2030s: the startups' timelines are credible
Never: fusion is always thirty years away

Neither hype nor cynicism: first-of-a-kind plants face the standard mega-project risks (materials, licensing, supply chains, cost overruns) — credible contribution means multiple operating plants with learning-curve cost declines, which the historical record of novel energy mega-projects puts in the 2040s at the optimistic end; price timelines against that base rate
The timeline does not matter: invest on vision
scenarios.why: The honest answer uses base rates: first-of-a-kind energy mega-projects historically overrun on time and budget, and 'contribution to the grid' means fleets with falling costs, not one demonstration. The 2040s-optimistic framing respects both the real progress (ignition, private capital, HTS magnets) and the real remaining work. Startup timelines are fundraising instruments; 'always thirty years' ignores the cost-curve evidence.
scenarios.hint: What does 'contribute to the grid' actually require?
objectives: Use base rates for mega-project timelines
Define 'contribution' as fleets with falling costs

scenarios.title: The HTS Bet
scenarios.situation: High-temperature superconducting magnets promise much stronger magnetic fields in compact tokamaks — the basis of several private ventures' designs.
scenarios.prompt: How should a technical reviewer evaluate the HTS claim?
choices: Accept it: stronger fields obviously solve confinement

Evaluate the full stack: HTS enables compact high-field designs, but the reviewer must check magnet durability under neutron flux, quench protection at scale, manufacturing maturity, and whether the compact size actually reduces plant cost or just plasma cost — magnets are one layer of the stack
Reject it: superconductors are laboratory curiosities
Evaluate only the field strength: the rest follows
scenarios.why: HTS is a genuine advance — high-field compact tokamaks are a real design space — but the stack lens applies: magnets sit inside a plant with neutron fluxes, maintenance needs, and balance-of-plant costs. Stronger fields do not solve tritium breeding or materials; compact plasma does not guarantee cheap electricity. Evaluate the layer, then the stack around it.
scenarios.hint: What does a compact tokamak still need besides magnets?
objectives: Evaluate HTS within the full plant stack
Check magnets against neutron and manufacturing reality
Separate plasma cost from plant cost
evidence: Neutrons, breeding, maintenance, balance of plant

scenarios.title: Stellarator vs Tokamak
scenarios.situation: A team proposes a stellarator, accepting its brutal magnet complexity in exchange for steady-state operation without plasma-current disruptions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the core trade-off being weighed?
choices: There is no trade-off: stellarators are strictly better

Engineering complexity now vs operational stability later: the stellarator's twisted magnets are enormously harder to design and build, but the payoff is intrinsically steady-state plasma free of tokamak disruptions — the bet is that computational design (which cracked stellarator optimization) has moved the complexity cost down enough
Stellarators cannot work: only tokamaks are physical
The trade-off is purely financial
scenarios.why: This is the honest stellarator thesis: pay in magnet complexity upfront for disruption-free steady state forever after — and the reason the thesis is newly credible is computational optimization, which solved design problems that were intractable by hand. The trade is engineering pain against operational grace, repriced by computation. 'Strictly better' ignores the build cost; 'cannot work' ignores the physics.
scenarios.hint: What changed to make the stellarator bet credible now?
objectives: Credit computational design for repricing the trade
Evaluate the full trade, not one side

scenarios.title: Fusion's Grid Role
scenarios.situation: Assume fusion plants work and reach competitive cost. A grid planner asks what role fusion plays in a grid already adding cheap solar, wind, and batteries.
scenarios.prompt: What is fusion's strategic grid value?
choices: None: renewables plus storage already solve everything

Firm, dispatchable, carbon-free baseload: fusion's value is not cheap electrons at noon but reliable electrons at midnight in winter — complementing variable renewables, displacing the last fossil firm capacity, and serving industrial heat and dense loads
Fusion replaces all renewables: one technology wins
Fusion is only for spacecraft: the grid does not need it
scenarios.why: The grid's hard problem is not cheap midday electrons but firm clean power through dark winters and industrial heat — exactly where variable renewables plus storage get expensive. Fusion's strategic role is firm dispatchable baseload in a deeply decarbonized grid, complementing rather than replacing renewables. 'One technology wins' misunderstands grids; 'renewables solve everything' ignores the firm-capacity problem.
scenarios.hint: What is the grid's hardest remaining problem?
objectives: Position fusion as firm clean baseload

domains.summary: Magnetic and inertial confinement paths to net energy.

scenarios.title: Choosing the Recording Modality
scenarios.situation: A BCI startup targeting assistive communication must choose: implanted microelectrode arrays (high bandwidth, surgery required) or non-invasive EEG (safe, low bandwidth).
choices: Bandwidth only: implants always win

The clinical risk-benefit for the target users: people with locked-in syndrome face a different calculus than healthy consumers — match invasiveness to the severity of need, the reversibility of the procedure, and the regulatory path, not to the engineering elegance
Cost only: EEG is cheaper to build
Speed to market only: pick whatever ships first
scenarios.why: Modality choice is clinical strategy, not engineering preference: the users who need BCIs most (paralysis, locked-in) justify invasive risk; healthy consumers do not — and regulators, ethicists, and users all price it that way. Bandwidth matters, but only inside the risk-benefit frame. Cost and speed are real constraints but subordinate to the clinical logic.
scenarios.hint: Whose brain, and what is at stake for them?

scenarios.title: The Decoder's Generalization Problem
scenarios.situation: Your BCI decoder achieves 95% accuracy on the training participant in the lab, but accuracy collapses when tested on a new participant.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the fix direction?
choices: The decoder is broken: rebuild from scratch

A generalization failure: neural signals vary substantially across individuals (and across days within one individual) — the fix direction is adaptive decoding (recalibration, transfer learning, day-to-day adaptation), larger diverse training data, and honest reporting of cross-subject performance
The new participant is unsuitable: screen harder
95% in-lab is sufficient: ship it
scenarios.why: Cross-subject and cross-day variability is the central fact of neural decoding — brains differ, electrodes drift, signals non-stationary. The field's progress is largely the story of adaptive decoders that recalibrate. Screening participants to flatter the metric is selection bias; shipping lab-only accuracy is how BCIs fail in the field.
scenarios.hint: What varies between the lab participant and the new one?
evidence: Neural variability across people and days

scenarios.title: Closing the Loop
scenarios.situation: Your motor BCI lets a user move a cursor. The team debates adding sensory feedback via cortical stimulation — a much harder problem.
choices: Skip it: open-loop control is sufficient

Bidirectional is the unlock: without feedback the user flies blind — closed-loop systems with sensory feedback dramatically improve control quality and embodiment, and the teams that solve stimulation own the next generation; the difficulty is the moat
Add it only if trivial: difficulty is a reason to avoid
Stimulation is unsafe by definition: never do it
scenarios.why: The field's direction is bidirectional: sensing plus stimulation, closed loop — because control without feedback is crippled, and embodiment (the device feeling like part of the body) requires afferent signal. The difficulty is real (safe, precise, meaningful stimulation is genuinely hard), which is exactly why solving it is the strategic moat. 'Unsafe by definition' ignores the entire therapeutic stimulation field.
scenarios.hint: What is the user missing in open-loop control?
objectives: Treat stimulation difficulty as the moat

scenarios.title: Neural Data Privacy
scenarios.situation: Your BCI collects high-resolution neural data. The product team wants to upload raw recordings to the cloud for model improvement; the ethics advisor objects.
choices: Upload everything: model improvement outweighs privacy

Treat neural data as the most sensitive data class that exists: minimize collection, process on-device where possible, encrypt and strictly govern what leaves the device, obtain genuinely informed consent for each use — neural data can reveal health conditions, intentions, and identity
Privacy is impossible anyway: give up
Anonymize by removing names: that suffices
scenarios.why: Neural data is uniquely sensitive — it can reveal neurological conditions, cognitive states, and potentially intentions; 'anonymized' neural signals can be re-identifiable. The resolution is data minimization plus on-device processing plus genuine consent, not maximalism and not surrender. Removing names from the most biometric data there is is not anonymization.
scenarios.hint: What could raw neural recordings reveal about a person?
objectives: Require genuine informed consent per use

scenarios.title: The Consumer BCI Pitch
scenarios.situation: A consumer startup promises 'telepathic messaging' via a headband, citing lab demos of decoded speech from implanted electrodes.
scenarios.prompt: What does the hype checklist say?
choices: Believe it: the lab demos prove the product

Flag the modality gap: the demos used invasive recordings with orders of magnitude more signal than a headband's EEG can capture — the pitch implies a transfer across modalities that the physics does not support; ask for headband-specific evidence
Dismiss BCIs entirely: nothing works
Invest immediately: first movers win
scenarios.why: The classic consumer-BCI sleight: cite invasive results, sell non-invasive product. The signal physics differ by orders of magnitude — implanted electrodes vs scalp EEG is not an engineering gap to be closed by enthusiasm, it is a different measurement. The checklist demands modality-matched evidence: show it working on the headband or the claim is unfounded.
scenarios.hint: What recording modality produced the cited demos?

scenarios.title: The Chronic Implant Problem
scenarios.situation: Your implanted array works beautifully at 6 months. At 2 years, signal quality has degraded significantly — the known tissue-response problem.
choices: Hide the degradation: report only the 6-month data

Face it as the central engineering challenge: invest in biocompatible materials, flexible electrodes, and signal-processing that adapts to drift — chronic stability is the difference between a demo and a therapy, and honest long-term data is the regulatory and clinical currency
Explant all devices at 6 months: declare victory
Blame the patients: their tissue is the problem
scenarios.why: Chronic stability is THE implant problem — the field knows tissue response degrades rigid arrays, and the therapy-vs-demo distinction turns on years of stable function. Hiding degradation is fraud-adjacent and regulatorily fatal; explanting at peak is theater. The strategic response is materials, mechanics, and adaptive decoding aimed at the multi-year horizon.
scenarios.hint: What separates a demo from a therapy?
objectives: Invest in biocompatibility and adaptive decoding
evidence: Signal degradation at 2 years: tissue response

scenarios.title: Agency and Identity
scenarios.situation: A long-term BCI user reports feeling that the device's predictive text 'puts words in my mouth' — they are unsure which thoughts are theirs.
scenarios.prompt: What does responsible BCI practice require?
choices: Dismiss it: the user is confused

Take agency effects as a first-class design and clinical consideration: study how predictive assistance affects the sense of agency, give users control over assistance levels, monitor for identity effects in long-term follow-up, and treat the user's report as safety data — not confusion
Increase the prediction aggressiveness: faster is better
Remove all assistance: pure decoding only
scenarios.why: Sense of agency is a safety endpoint, not a philosophical luxury: if users cannot distinguish their intentions from the device's predictions, the system has an agency problem that design must address — adjustable assistance, transparency about predictions, long-term monitoring. Dismissing the report discards safety data; maximizing prediction maximizes the problem.
scenarios.hint: Who authored the sentence: the user or the decoder?
objectives: Treat agency as a safety endpoint
evidence: Agency effects as design + clinical data

scenarios.title: The BCI Roadmap Bet
scenarios.situation: You are advising a foundation's 10-year BCI portfolio: concentrate on invasive high-bandwidth approaches, or spread across invasive, non-invasive, and stimulation?
choices: Concentrate: one bet, maximum force

Spread across the stack with theses: invasive for severe clinical need (risk justified), non-invasive for broad wellness and research (scale), stimulation/bidirectional as the long-term unlock — each with its own success metric, because they serve different populations and mature on different clocks
Fund only non-invasive: safety first, always
Fund only what is nearest to market
scenarios.why: BCIs are not one technology but a stack serving different populations: the portfolio matches modality to need and clock — invasive for locked-in patients now, non-invasive for scale, bidirectional as the generational bet. Concentration gambles the foundation's decade on one clock; nearest-market-only abandons the severe-need patients who justify the field.
scenarios.hint: Which population does each modality serve, and on what clock?
objectives: Match modality to population and clock
Give each track its own success metric

domains.name: Autonomous Systems

scenarios.title: The Perception Stack Bet
scenarios.situation: An autonomous trucking startup debates perception: lidar-heavy stack vs camera-only with advanced neural networks.
scenarios.prompt: How should the decision be made?
choices: Camera-only: lidar is a crutch and vision will win
Lidar-heavy: only lidar is safe

On operational grounds: evaluate against the operating domain (highway trucking is geometrically simpler than urban), redundancy requirements, cost at fleet scale, and failure modes in the specific conditions (rain, dust, night) — the right stack follows the ODD, not ideology
Whichever the founders prefer: conviction matters most
scenarios.why: Perception architecture follows the operational design domain: highway trucking's structured environment changes the sensor calculus versus urban robotaxis, and fleet-scale cost, redundancy, and weather performance decide — not tribal affiliation. 'Lidar is a crutch' and 'only lidar is safe' are both slogans; the ODD analysis is engineering.
scenarios.hint: What is this system actually driving through?
evidence: ODD fit, redundancy, fleet cost, weather

scenarios.title: The Safety Case
scenarios.situation: Regulators ask your autonomous system for its safety case before expanded deployment. The team proposes submitting miles-driven statistics.
scenarios.prompt: What does a real safety case require?
choices: Miles driven is sufficient: more miles means safer

A structured safety argument: hazard analysis, ODD definition, verification and validation evidence across simulation, closed-course, and public-road testing, disengagement and incident analysis, redundancy architecture, and a credible claim about residual risk — miles are one input, not the case
A promise to be careful: regulators accept intent
No safety case is needed: innovation requires freedom
scenarios.why: Miles without structure prove exposure, not safety: the safety case is a structured argument — hazards identified, ODD bounded, V&V evidence across test regimes, incidents analyzed, redundancies demonstrated, residual risk quantified. This is how aviation and other safety-critical industries work, and autonomy is joining them. Statistics alone are the oldest trick in the book.
scenarios.hint: What would convince a skeptical engineer, not just a regulator?
evidence: Hazard analysis, V&V, ODD, incident analysis

scenarios.title: The Edge Case Long Tail
scenarios.situation: Your autonomous system handles 99.9% of scenarios in its ODD. Leadership wants to launch, arguing the remaining 0.1% is negligible.
choices: Launch: 99.9% is excellent

The long tail is the product: at fleet scale, 0.1% of millions of miles is thousands of edge cases — the remaining scenarios concentrate the hardest, weirdest, most dangerous situations, and handling them (detection, graceful degradation, remote assistance) IS the deployment engineering
The 0.1% will never occur: ignore it
Launch but hide the 0.1% from regulators
scenarios.why: Autonomy's cruel math: the last fraction of scenarios contains the concentrated weirdness — and at scale, rare becomes routine. Deployment engineering is largely edge-case engineering: minimal-risk maneuvers, remote assistance, graceful degradation. Launching on the 99.9% without the tail plan is how deployments become incidents.
scenarios.hint: At a million miles a week, what is 0.1%?
objectives: Scale rare into routine in your math

scenarios.title: The Handoff Problem
scenarios.situation: Your Level 3 highway system requires the driver to take over within 10 seconds when it disengages. Testing shows drivers need 15-30 seconds to regain situational awareness.
choices: Ship it: drivers will adapt with experience

The handoff design is unsafe by measurement: human-factors data shows takeover times exceed the budget — redesign toward longer budgets, better driver monitoring, minimal-risk maneuvers the system executes itself, or a different automation level; the measured human is the spec
Blame the drivers: they should pay attention
Reduce the budget to 5 seconds to force alertness
scenarios.why: Human-factors measurements are specifications, not suggestions: if drivers need 15-30 seconds, a 10-second handoff budget is a designed failure. The fixes are system-level — monitoring, graceful self-handling, honest automation levels — not exhortation. 'Drivers will adapt' is how the handoff problem has killed people in aviation and driving alike.
scenarios.hint: What does the measurement say the system must do?

scenarios.title: Simulation vs Reality
scenarios.situation: Your team validates almost entirely in simulation, which is fast and cheap. Real-world testing is minimal.
choices: None: simulation is sufficient

The sim-to-real gap: simulation validates against modeled worlds — unmodeled phenomena (sensor dirt, bizarre human behavior, novel objects) live in reality, so validation needs the triad — simulation for scale, closed-course for control, public-road for reality — with continuous calibration between them
Simulation is useless: test only in reality
The gap does not exist for good simulators
scenarios.why: Simulation is necessary and insufficient: it gives scale but only against what modelers imagined — reality's long tail is unmodeled by definition. The industry standard is the triad with calibration loops: sim finds candidate issues, closed-course tests controllably, public road confronts reality, and discrepancies feed back into the sim. Sim-only validation is confidence without contact.
scenarios.hint: What lives in reality that no modeler imagined?

scenarios.title: Autonomy Economics
scenarios.situation: Your robotaxi unit economics show profitability at scale, assuming 20-hour daily utilization and remote-assistance ratios of 1:50.
choices: Nothing: the model is the model

The assumptions: utilization under real demand patterns and charging/maintenance downtime, assistance ratios in the long-tail ODD (ratios collapse when edge cases cluster), insurance and incident costs, and fleet operations overhead — autonomy economics are won or lost in the assumptions, and the tail eats the margin
Only the vehicle cost: that dominates
Raise prices: economics follow
scenarios.why: Autonomy business models die in the assumptions: utilization is never the brochure number once charging, cleaning, and maintenance enter; assistance ratios measured in easy miles collapse in hard ones; one incident reprices insurance. The strategist's job is adversarial review of the spreadsheet — because the long tail does not just challenge the engineering, it eats the margin.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the 1:50 ratio during a rainstorm at rush hour?
objectives: Model assistance ratios under tail conditions

scenarios.title: Dual-Use Autonomy
scenarios.situation: Your perception and planning stack has obvious defense applications. A defense contract would fund the company for years; the team is divided.
choices: Take it: funding is funding
Refuse on principle: no discussion

Decide explicitly and document: run the dual-use review — what the tech enables, how it changes the harm landscape, what the team's values and the company's charter say, what employee and public response will be — and make the decision a deliberate, communicated policy, not a drift
Take it secretly: avoid the debate
scenarios.why: Dual-use decisions demand deliberateness: the ethics lesson's review applies — capability assessment, values alignment, stakeholder consequences — made explicitly and communicated, whichever way it goes. 'Funding is funding' abdicates judgment; blanket refusal without review abdicates it too; secrecy guarantees the worst version of the debate later. Decide like it matters, because it does.
scenarios.hint: What would you want the decision memo to say in five years?
objectives: Align decision with charter and values

scenarios.title: The Deployment Sequence
scenarios.situation: You can deploy in one easy geofenced downtown, or attempt three cities at once for the bigger announcement.
choices: Three cities: bigger announcements attract more capital

One domain, deeply: expand the ODD only when the safety case, operations, and economics are proven in the current domain — autonomy deployments succeed by deepening before widening, because each new domain resets the long tail
Deploy everywhere at once: speed wins markets
Never deploy: the tail is infinite
scenarios.why: Each new operational domain is a new long tail: new weather, new road users, new edge cases — widening before the current domain is mastered multiplies unknown unknowns. The disciplined sequence is deepen-then-widen: prove safety case, operations, and economics in one ODD, then expand deliberately. Announcement size is not a deployment criterion.
scenarios.hint: What resets when you enter a new city?
objectives: Prove safety, ops, economics per domain

domains.summary: Perception, planning, and control for autonomy.

domains.name: Synthetic Biology

scenarios.title: The Parts Registry Bet
scenarios.situation: Your team debates investing in characterizing standardized biological parts (promoters, regulators) versus pushing ahead with bespoke designs for each project.
scenarios.prompt: What does the engineering-biology lens say?
choices: Bespoke always: biology is too contextual for standards

Standards are the platform: characterized, reusable parts with known behavior are what turn craft into engineering — the upfront characterization cost pays back across every future design, and the field's history (BioBricks onward) shows platforms beat one-offs
Standards are a waste: move fast with bespoke
Outsource the decision: let the funders choose
scenarios.why: Engineering disciplines are built on standardized parts with characterized behavior — biology's context-dependence makes this harder, not less valuable. The bespoke path feels faster per project but never compounds; the parts path builds the platform every design reuses. BioBricks' lesson stands: characterize once, compose forever.
scenarios.hint: What compounds across projects: bespoke designs or characterized parts?
objectives: Build the platform, not just the product
evidence: Parts registry vs bespoke per project

scenarios.title: The DBTL Cycle
scenarios.situation: Your strain-engineering program runs design-build-test-learn cycles that take 8 weeks each. Leadership wants faster results and proposes skipping the 'learn' step to save time.
choices: Skip learn: testing is what matters

The learn step IS the acceleration: without systematic learning from each cycle — models updated, hypotheses revised — the program repeats experiments instead of compounding knowledge; the way to go faster is automating and parallelizing the full cycle, not amputating it
Slow down further: speed is the enemy
Outsource the whole cycle
scenarios.why: DBTL without L is just DBT — expensive repetition. The learn step converts each cycle's data into better next designs; skipping it trades the appearance of speed for the reality of stagnation. Real acceleration comes from foundry automation running full cycles in parallel — faster loops, not broken ones.
scenarios.hint: What does the program know after ten cycles without learning?

scenarios.title: The Screening Decision
scenarios.situation: Your DNA synthesis foundry receives an order for a sequence that screening flags as a potential pathogen component. The customer is insistent and the order is large.
choices: Fill it: the customer is always right

Refuse and report: synthesis screening is the industry's front line against bioweapon proliferation — the International Gene Synthesis Consortium norms exist precisely for this; no order size overrides the screening decision, and the refusal is documented and reported through proper channels
Fill it quietly: screening is overcautious
Ask the customer to reword the order
scenarios.why: This is the biosecurity lesson's core scenario: synthesis screening is where the dual-use rubber meets the road, and the norms hold only if foundries hold them under commercial pressure. A large insistent order for a flagged sequence is exactly the case the screening regime was built for. Document, refuse, report.
scenarios.hint: What is synthesis screening FOR?
objectives: Hold the screening line under pressure
Treat norms as binding, not optional

scenarios.title: From Bench to Bioreactor
scenarios.situation: Your engineered strain produces a valuable compound at 1 mL bench scale. Investors want the 10,000 L scale-up timeline.
scenarios.prompt: What does honest scale-up planning include?
choices: Bench results scale linearly: multiply by ten million

The scale-up valley: oxygen transfer, mixing, heat removal, contamination risk, and strain stability all change with scale — honest planning includes pilot stages (bench -> pilot -> demo -> commercial), kill criteria at each stage, and timelines measured in years with named technical risks
Skip pilot: go straight to commercial
Scale-up is someone else's problem
scenarios.why: Biology does not scale linearly: transport phenomena, contamination, and evolution all change with volume, and the honest path runs staged pilots with kill criteria. 'Multiply by ten million' is innumeracy; skipping pilot is how capital is incinerated. The strain that wins at 1 mL must be re-proven at every scale.
scenarios.hint: What changes between 1 mL and 10,000 L?
objectives: Plan staged scale-up with kill criteria

scenarios.title: The Cell-Free Option
scenarios.situation: Your team needs to prototype 200 genetic circuit variants quickly. The cell-based pipeline manages 20 per month.
scenarios.prompt: What does the cell-free approach offer, and what are its limits?
choices: Nothing: cell-free is a toy

Speed and parallelism: cell-free systems (lysates or purified components) prototype circuits in hours without cloning or cell culture — ideal for screening 200 variants fast; the limit is that cell-free results do not always transfer to living cells, so it screens candidates rather than replacing cell-based validation
Cell-free replaces all cell work permanently
Avoid it: unfamiliar methods are risky
scenarios.why: Cell-free is the rapid-prototyping layer of synthetic biology: hours instead of weeks, massive parallelism — but it is a screen, not a substitute, because cellular context (growth, regulation, burden) changes circuit behavior. The disciplined pipeline is cell-free for breadth, cells for validation. 200 variants at 20/month is a ten-month queue; cell-free collapses it to weeks.
scenarios.hint: What does cell-free screening buy, and what does it not prove?
objectives: Use cell-free for rapid variant screening

scenarios.title: The IP Strategy
scenarios.situation: Your synbio startup must choose: patent the engineered pathway aggressively, or open-source the parts and sell the foundry service.
choices: Patents always: IP is the only moat
Open always: information wants to be free

The business model decides: patent where the moat is the molecule (therapeutics, novel compounds), open the platform where the moat is execution speed and foundry scale — and note the biosecurity overlay: some sequences should not be openly published regardless of business logic
IP does not matter in synbio
scenarios.why: IP strategy follows the moat: molecule-moats patent, execution-moats open the platform to drive volume. And synthetic biology carries the biosecurity constraint that overrides business logic — dual-use sequences stay out of open registries. 'Patents always' strangles platforms; 'open always' ignores both moats and misuse risk.
scenarios.hint: Where is this company's actual moat?
objectives: Match IP strategy to the moat

scenarios.title: The Burden Problem
scenarios.situation: Your engineered circuit works on day one but the strain evolves away from production within 50 generations — the metabolic burden selects against your design.
choices: Accept it: evolution always wins, so synbio is futile

Design for evolution: reduce burden (efficient parts, burden-aware design), add stability mechanisms (addiction modules, genome integration vs plasmid), and treat evolutionary stability as a design specification — the circuit must survive selection, not just function on day one
Restart the culture every week: outrun evolution operationally
Hide the data: report only day-one results
scenarios.why: Evolution is a design constraint, not a refutation: production strains must be evolutionarily stable, which means burden minimization and stability engineering are core design specs — the best circuit on day one that dies by generation 50 is a failed design. Operational outrunning is a treadmill; hiding data is fraud. Design for selection.
scenarios.hint: What selects against your circuit?

scenarios.title: Platform vs Product
scenarios.situation: Your foundry can either sell custom strain-engineering services (product work) or invest in becoming the platform others build on.
choices: Services: cash now is all that matters
Platform: winner-take-all dynamics reward the standard

The sequencing matters: services fund the platform — run high-margin custom work to finance the automation, data, and parts characterization that become the platform, then productize the platform; pure-platform bets starve, pure-services bets never compound
Neither: synbio has no viable business
scenarios.why: The false choice is services OR platform: services generate the cash, data, and characterized parts that the platform is built from — the winners sequence them. Pure platform without revenue starves before the flywheel spins; pure services caps at labor. The strategy is services-funded platform building, with the platform as the compounding asset.
scenarios.hint: What does the platform get built from?

domains.summary: Engineering biology: from parts to platforms.

domains.name: Edge Computing and 6G

scenarios.title: Workload Placement
scenarios.situation: Your application has three components: real-time control (5 ms budget), video analytics (100 ms budget), and nightly model retraining (no deadline).
scenarios.prompt: Where does each belong on the device-edge-cloud continuum?
choices: All in the cloud: centralization is simplest

Control on-device (deterministic latency), analytics at the near edge (regional, low latency, cheap bandwidth), retraining in the cloud (elastic compute, no deadline) — place by latency budget, bandwidth cost, and compute elasticity
All on-device: the cloud is a liability
Place randomly: the orchestrator will sort it out
scenarios.why: Placement follows physics and economics: the 5 ms control loop cannot survive a network round trip — it lives on-device; analytics wants near-edge (latency plus bandwidth savings); retraining wants cloud elasticity. 'All cloud' fails the control loop; 'all device' wastes the cloud's elasticity; the continuum exists to be used discriminately.
scenarios.hint: What breaks if the control loop goes to the cloud?
objectives: Use each tier for its strengths
evidence: 5 ms control / 100 ms analytics / batch retraining

scenarios.title: The 6G Investment Question
scenarios.situation: A carrier asks whether to invest heavily in 6G R&D now or wait for the standard to mature. The 5G ROI is still incomplete.
choices: Invest now: first movers always win
Wait: 6G is pure hype

Evaluate the use-case pull: 6G's promised capabilities (sub-ms latency, sensing-plus-communication, AI-native air interface) must map to revenue-grade use cases the carrier can actually sell — invest proportional to validated demand, hedge with software-upgradeable infrastructure, and learn from the 5G ROI shortfall
Copy competitors: whatever they do
scenarios.why: Generational wireless investment is use-case arithmetic: 5G's ROI lesson is that capability without sellable applications strands capital. 6G's distinctive promises (integrated sensing, AI-native networks, extreme latency) need validated demand before heavy R&D — invest in optionality (upgradeable infrastructure, targeted research) proportional to evidence, not to the generation number.
scenarios.hint: What did 5G teach about capability vs revenue?
objectives: Demand use-case pull for generational bets
evidence: 5G: capability deployed ahead of sellable apps

scenarios.title: The Latency Budget
scenarios.situation: Your autonomous system's latency budget is 20 ms end-to-end. The team assumes 'the edge' will handle it without specifying which edge.
choices: Nothing: edge means fast

A real budget: decompose the 20 ms across sensing, uplink, compute, downlink, and actuation — then verify each segment against the actual edge tier (on-device vs far edge vs regional), because 'the edge' spans three orders of magnitude in latency and only the decomposition tells you which tier qualifies
More budget: 20 ms is too tight
Less edge: do it all on-device
scenarios.why: 'The edge' is not a latency guarantee — it is a continuum from on-device microseconds to regional tens of milliseconds. The missing work is the decomposition: allocate milliseconds per segment, then match segments to tiers. Undifferentiated 'edge will handle it' is how latency budgets die in production.
scenarios.hint: How many milliseconds does each segment get?
objectives: Match segments to specific edge tiers

scenarios.title: Edge Security Model
scenarios.situation: Your edge deployment puts compute in hundreds of physically accessible locations — retail stores, cell towers, factory floors.
scenarios.prompt: What does the threat model change?
choices: Nothing: same as cloud security

Everything about physical trust: assume physical access by adversaries — encrypt data at rest and in use (confidential computing where available), attest device integrity remotely, design for device compromise (revocation, key rotation), and minimize sensitive data at the edge
Edge cannot be secured: abandon the project
Physical security guards at every site: the only answer
scenarios.why: Edge inverts cloud's physical-security assumption: the data center's locked cage becomes a hundred accessible closets. The model shifts to zero-trust hardware — attestation, encryption everywhere, compromise-ready key management, data minimization. Guards at every tower is not a security architecture; abandonment ignores that the model is solvable.
scenarios.hint: Who can touch the edge device?
objectives: Attest and encrypt; plan for compromise

scenarios.title: Network Slicing Strategy
scenarios.situation: A 5G/6G carrier offers your industrial automation firm a dedicated network slice with guaranteed latency.
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the offer?
choices: Accept: guaranteed latency solves everything

Evaluate the guarantee's substance: what latency at what percentile, under what load, with what remedies for breach — then compare against your decomposed budget and against private-network alternatives; a slice is a contract, and contracts are read before signing
Reject: slices are marketing
Accept but never verify: trust the carrier
scenarios.why: Network slicing's value is contractual: the question is what the SLA actually guarantees (percentiles, conditions, remedies) versus your application's decomposed needs — and versus building private. 'Guaranteed latency' without percentiles is a slogan. Evaluate, compare, verify continuously — the slice is only as good as its enforcement.
scenarios.hint: What does the SLA guarantee, exactly?
objectives: Read the slice SLA as a contract

scenarios.title: Edge Economics
scenarios.situation: Your CFO notes edge infrastructure costs more per compute unit than cloud, and asks why not centralize everything.
scenarios.prompt: What is the economic defense of edge?
choices: There is none: centralize

Total-cost arithmetic: edge trades higher compute unit cost for lower latency (revenue-enabling), lower backhaul bandwidth cost (video at scale), and regulatory/compliance wins (data residency) — the defense is workload-specific: show which workloads' economics flip at the edge, and centralize the rest
Edge is always cheaper: assert it confidently
The CFO is wrong about the numbers: argue
scenarios.why: Edge economics are workload-specific, not ideological: per-unit compute costs more at the edge, but bandwidth savings (not backhauling petabytes of video), latency-enabled revenue, and data-residency compliance flip specific workloads' total cost. The honest answer centralizes what centralizes well and edges what edges well — with the math shown per workload.
scenarios.hint: Which workloads' total cost flips at the edge?
objectives: Argue total cost, not unit cost

scenarios.title: Offline Resilience
scenarios.situation: Your edge application serves a factory that occasionally loses backhaul connectivity for hours.
choices: Nothing: outages are the carrier's problem

Autonomous operation: the edge tier must run the critical workloads standalone — local control loops, local data buffering with sync-on-reconnect, degraded-mode operation defined in advance — because the factory cannot stop when the backhaul does
Shut down during outages: safety first
Pray for better carriers
scenarios.why: Edge's promise includes resilience: when the backhaul drops, the edge keeps the factory running — but only if designed for it. Autonomous degraded modes, local buffering, and sync-on-reconnect are architecture, not accident. 'Carrier's problem' is abdication; shutdown-by-default wastes the edge's whole value proposition.
scenarios.hint: What keeps running when the backhaul drops?

scenarios.title: 6G's Killer App
scenarios.situation: Asked to name 6G's killer app, your team lists: faster phones, better video, and 'the metaverse'.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this list?
choices: Nothing: those are the apps

It is 5G's list with bigger numbers: 6G's distinctive capabilities are integrated sensing-and-communication, AI-native network optimization, and sub-ms deterministic latency for industrial control — the killer apps likely live in industrial automation, digital twins with real-time sync, and ambient sensing, not in faster consumer video
6G has no apps: it is pointless
The killer app is known: it is holographic calls
scenarios.why: Generational killer apps never look like 'faster previous generation': 4G's was not faster 3G-video but the app economy and ride-sharing; 6G's distinctive bets (sensing-plus-communication, AI-native air interface, deterministic latency) point at industrial and ambient applications. Listing consumer video is imagining the future as the present, faster.
scenarios.hint: What can 6G do that 5G fundamentally cannot?
objectives: Look for distinctive capabilities, not faster ones

lessons.title: The Frontier Path — Core concepts
concepts: The frontier is compositional: its hardest problems are not in any single domain but in their intersections — feedback loops around AI systems, persuasion delivered by imitating machines, zero-trust architectures for non-human agents, undecidability limits on AI assurance. Learn the domains so you can combine them.

Proxy metrics plus feedback loops equal Goodhart machines: any measure optimized in a loop (satisfaction scores steering a chatbot, engagement steering a recommender) decouples from the goal it shadows. Frontier engineering puts the actual goal — or an audited proxy — in the loop, with negative feedback against drift.

Imitation composes with credibility: a system that passes behavioral tests for humanness (Turing's criterion) inherits the persuasion dynamics Bernays mapped (borrowed trust converts to belief). Defending against synthetic persuasion requires verifying the speaker (provenance) and auditing the message (literacy) together.

Computability sets the ceiling on assurance: Rice's theorem (1953) — non-trivial semantic properties of arbitrary programs are undecidable — rules out universal AI verifiers. Assurance must be layered: verified restricted classes, testing, monitoring, and process audit, honestly priced.

Ethics at the frontier is architectural: deontological duties as hard constraints (autonomy, non-manipulation), utilitarian optimization within them, Rawls' veil as the admissibility test for self-serving rules, and cybernetic monitoring of what the system actually does. Frameworks are components; the stack is the position.

Emergence is the frontier's recurring formal pattern — global order from local rules without a blueprint, from reaction-diffusion spots to stable control loops to unprogrammed model capabilities. The pattern unifies; the mechanism in each case still has to be earned. Synthesis without mechanism is mysticism with better vocabulary.

example.code:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# Goodhart demo: optimize the proxy, lose the goal
# goal = helpfulness, proxy = user rating (rewards agreement)
import random
random.seed(7)
for agree_bias in (0.0, 0.5, 0.9):
    rating = sum(1 for _ in range(1000) if random.random() < 0.5 + agree_bias*0.5)/1000
    helpful = 0.8 - agree_bias*0.5   # sycophancy erodes real helpfulness
    print(f"agree_bias={agree_bias}: rating={rating:.2f} helpfulness={helpful:.2f}")
print("The metric rises while the goal falls: the loop optimizes the shadow.")
EOF
example.walkthrough: As agreeableness bias rises, ratings climb and true helpfulness falls — the proxy decouples from the goal. This is the quantitative shape of every Goodhart failure: the loop is working perfectly, on the wrong thing.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating any single domain as sufficient — the frontier's characteristic failures (sycophantic loops, synthetic persuasion, agent privilege) are all compositional; single-domain thinking misses them.
Common trap: demanding universal guarantees where computability forbids them — no verifier, audit, or test suite decides arbitrary behavioral properties; design for layered assurance instead.
Common trap: optimizing the metric instead of the goal — if the loop's sensor measures a proxy, the system will become excellent at the proxy and mediocre at the purpose.
Common trap: using 'emergence' as an explanation — it names the pattern (global order from local rules); the explanation is still the specific mechanism, which must be found case by case.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Frontier Path move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of The Frontier Path
concepts: The Frontier Path is a multi-step process within The Frontier Path: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect The Frontier Path to the broader The Frontier Path ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  The Frontier Path begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to The Frontier Path. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating The Frontier Path as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here, then each domain in sequence, then the mock assessment. Skipping ahead breaks the scaffolding the later material assumes.
What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands. Every lab in this course runs there — no GUI needed.
Scenarios are decision drills: read the situation, commit to an answer, then study the explanation. The explanation is the real lesson.
Your progress saves automatically. A domain unlocks fully when you engage with its lessons, scenarios, and labs — depth beats speed.

LEARN → PRACTICE → PROVE

  2. Run the terminal lab (hands-on reps)
  3. Answer the scenarios (decision drills)
  4. Finish with the mock assessment (timed, exam-style)

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping straight to scenarios — the scenarios assume the lesson vocabulary.
Treating the terminal labs as optional — muscle memory is what survives exam pressure.
Rushing. Spaced, deliberate reps beat one marathon session.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for The Frontier Path
concepts: Time-box your sessions: 50 minutes of focused work, 10 minutes off. Three focused sessions beat one exhausted six-hour grind.
Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close it and explain the key idea out loud in your own words before moving on.
The frontier technology assessment rewards pattern recognition. Every scenario you answer builds a mental library of 'I've seen this shape before.'
Track your weak domains explicitly. Revisit them with the systems-anatomy lens: trace the full flow, find where your mental model breaks.

WEEKLY RHYTHM (example)

  Tue/Thu: scenario drills on prior domains
  Sat: timed mock assessment
  Sun: review misses, rebuild weak areas
example.walkthrough: Elite performers don't study more hours — they study with tighter feedback loops. Every wrong answer is a precise map of what to fix next.

pitfalls: Passive highlighting and re-reading — feels productive, builds nothing.
Avoiding timed practice until 'ready' — the clock is a skill, train it early.
Studying only strengths — comfort is the enemy of growth.

lessons.title: The Frontier Path: Field Overview
concepts: The big picture first: The Frontier Path sits at the intersection of theory you must know and judgment you must demonstrate.
Employers and examiners test the same thing: can you reason from first principles when the situation is novel, not just recite facts?
Every domain in this bootcamp maps to a real capability: something you will actually do, decide, or explain on the job.
The capstone at the end proves you can integrate everything — that is the artifact you show, not just talk about.

MAP OF THE TERRITORY

pitfalls: Treating domains as isolated trivia — they connect. Always ask how this domain touches the others.
Ignoring the 'why' behind procedures — procedures change, principles don't.
Waiting until the end to attempt the capstone — start scoping it now.

Taking the mock once — take it repeatedly until your score stabilizes above target.

lessons.title: Capstone: Frontier Thesis — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Produce a rigorous frontier thesis: pick one frontier domain, map its state of the art, identify the key bottlenecks, and argue where the next breakthrough comes from — with evidence.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

CAPSTONE MILESTONES
  1. Select a frontier domain and survey the state of the art
  2. Map the key technical bottlenecks with specificity
  3. Identify the leading approaches to each bottleneck
  4. Argue your breakthrough thesis with evidence
  5. Defend it in a 20-minute presentation with Q&A
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

pitfalls: Scope creep — freezing the milestone list on day one protects you.
Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'
