simulations.title: The Wedged Pipeline
simulations.brief: A hybrid system — symbolic reasoner feeding a neural ranker — has silently degraded. Diagnose across the boundary.

steps.symptom: End-to-end accuracy fell from 91% to 74% over two weeks. Neither component's unit tests fail.
evidence: Input distribution drift: 18% of fields now arrive null
No schema validation between the two components
options: Retrain the ranker — the model is obviously stale
The interface failed, not either component: the reasoner started emitting nulls the ranker never saw in training, and nothing validates the handoff
Add more training data to the ranker
steps.explain: Frontier systems fail at boundaries. Each side passes its own tests; the contract between them was never specified or validated. Fix the interface (schema + validation), then decide if retraining is needed.

steps.symptom: You add contract validation. Accuracy recovers to 89% but 6% of requests now hard-fail.
evidence: All from the reasoner emitting a new field the contract rejects
A knowledge-base update added the field last Tuesday
Failures cluster in one customer segment
options: Version the contract: accept the new field, validate its shape, and let the ranker declare which contract version it was trained against
Disable validation — 89% with failures is worse than 74% silent
steps.explain: Interfaces evolve; version them. The contract becomes a declared, tested artifact with versions, and each consumer pins the version it understands. Silent degradation becomes explicit negotiation.

steps.symptom: Fixed and versioned. What permanent practice prevents the next cross-boundary silent failure?
evidence: Must catch interface drift before it reaches production
Neither team can break the other silently again
options: Merge both teams into one so there's no boundary
Contract tests in CI on both sides plus production monitoring on the interface's input distribution
steps.explain: Consumer-driven contract tests in CI catch drift at build time; distribution monitoring catches it at runtime. The boundary is permanent — make it explicit and guarded instead of pretending it away.

simulations.debrief: Synthesis systems are boundary systems: computability meets control theory at an interface, and interfaces need contracts, versions, tests, and monitoring. Debug the boundary first.

simulations.title: Choose the Research Bet
simulations.brief: You have one year and a small team. Three frontier directions compete. Place the bet like a researcher, not a gambler.

steps.text: Three proposals: (A) neuro-symbolic theorem proving, (B) LLM agents for infrastructure automation, (C) formal verification of smart contracts. Your team: two strong engineers, one mathematician. Which do you fund?

choices.label: B — agents are hot, hiring and hype follow heat
choices.feedback: Heat is not edge. Your team has no infra-ops depth, and the space is crowded with better-funded labs. You'd be the tenth team doing the obvious thing.

choices.label: A — it matches the team's rare combination (math + engineering) and few teams sit at that intersection
choices.feedback: Edge comes from the intersection: the mathematician formalizes, the engineers build, and almost nobody else has both in one small team. Asymmetric bet.

choices.label: C — smart contracts are lucrative and verification is rigorous
choices.feedback: Respectable, but your team's mathematician does analysis, not formal methods — a six-month ramp before real output. The edge is thinner than it looks.

steps.text: Six months in: a frontier lab ships an open agent framework that does 80% of your roadmap. Your runway is half gone. Pivot or persist?

choices.label: Persist — our implementation will be better
choices.feedback: 'Better' against a frontier lab's distribution is not a strategy. The remaining runway buys a graceful pivot, not a heroic last stand.

choices.label: Pivot to the evaluation layer: everyone needs to measure these agents, nobody does it well
choices.feedback: The heat created a new adjacent gap — measurement. Your engineering strength transfers; the crowded lane is abandoned for the empty one next to it.

steps.text: The mathematician is ramping on formal methods but progress is slow. A DeFi protocol offers a paid audit that would fund 4 more months. Take it?

choices.label: Take it — runway is runway
choices.feedback: The audit consumes the mathematician for two months and teaches the team nothing about the research bet. You've traded the mission for money.

choices.label: Decline — protect the research calendar; the bet was the bet
choices.feedback: Discipline: the audit pays cash but costs the compounding that was the whole point. Saying no to revenue is the researcher's hardest skill.

steps.text: Month eight: the neuro-symbolic prover beats the baseline on 60% of benchmarks but fails weirdly on the rest — the neural guesser and symbolic checker disagree in ways nobody predicted. What's the move?

choices.label: Tune the neural guesser harder — the failures are noise
choices.feedback: The disagreements aren't noise; they're the discovery. Tuning past them buries the actual finding.

choices.label: Study the disagreements as the research object — characterize exactly when symbolic checking rejects neural guesses
choices.feedback: That's the contribution: a taxonomy of neuro-symbolic disagreement modes. The failure analysis IS the paper. Frontier work is found at the boundary, again.

simulations.debrief: Research bets are placed on team-shape fit and empty intersections, not heat. And the finding is usually hiding in the disagreement between your components — study the boundary.

simulations.title: Assemble the Frontier Stack
simulations.brief: Order the build sequence for a frontier synthesis system — from foundations to the question-keeping layer.

steps.context: You're building a system where computability theory, control theory, and AI engineering meet. Order the layers bottom-up.
items: Formalize the problem: what is computable here, and what are the control objectives
Build the symbolic core: the rules, invariants, and verifiable kernel
Add the learning layer: models that guess, constrained by the symbolic core
Instrument the boundaries: contracts, monitoring, and disagreement logging
Add the philosophy layer: the open questions the system must keep asking, not answer

simulations.debrief: Formalize first (know what's computable), symbolize second (the verifiable kernel), learn third (guesses inside constraints), instrument fourth (boundaries are where truth lives), and keep the philosophical questions open last — they steer the next iteration.

simulations.title: Audit the Agent Config
simulations.brief: An AI agent's production config is one incident away from autonomy it shouldn't have. Find the 3 dangerous settings.

steps.config:
# agent.conf — production
max_tool_calls = 50            # line 2
human_approval = none          # line 3
allowed_tools = read-only      # line 4
memory_retention = 90d        # line 5
prompt_source = user_input     # line 6
rate_limit = 100/min          # line 7
action_scope = production-db   # line 8

issues.description: No human approval required — the agent can act autonomously in production with 50 tool calls.
issues.fix: human_approval = required for all write/destructive actions.

issues.description: Prompt sourced directly from user input with no sanitization — prompt injection goes straight to the agent.
issues.fix: prompt_source = sanitized template; treat user input as data, never as instructions.

issues.description: Action scope includes the production database paired with no approval — the blast radius is the crown jewels.
issues.fix: action_scope = staging; production requires approval + break-glass procedure.

simulations.debrief: Lines 2, 4, 5, 7 are bounded and defensible. The lethal combination is autonomy (line 3) + unsanitized input (line 6) + production scope (line 8). Frontier engineering is largely the discipline of refusing dangerous defaults.

simulations.title: The Dual-Use Review
simulations.brief: Your persuasion-detection research could defend elections — or optimize manipulation. The review board is waiting.

steps.text: Your paper: a model that predicts which messages persuade which demographics. Defensive use: inoculation campaigns. Offensive use: micro-targeted manipulation. A defense contractor wants to license it. Your call?

choices.label: License it — research wants to be used, and the funding is real
choices.feedback: The capability diffuses to whoever pays most. You've built the targeting engine for the next influence operation and called it research.

choices.label: Publish the defense half openly; withhold the targeting optimization
choices.feedback: Differential publication: the inoculation methods go public, the persuasion optimizer stays in the lab notebook. Defense diffuses faster than offense.

choices.label: Bury the whole project — too dangerous to exist
choices.feedback: Someone else will build it within two years, and without your defensive insights. Burial doesn't prevent the capability; it only prevents the defense.

steps.text: A year later, your licensee's tooling appears in a documented election-interference campaign. Journalists call you for comment. What do you say?

choices.label: 'We couldn't have known.'
choices.feedback: You could have — the dual use was obvious at the review. The honest statement is harder and the only one available.

choices.label: 'We licensed it; the misuse is real; here's the defensive toolkit we should have led with.'
choices.feedback: Accountability plus the defense you should have published first. Late, but it's the only move that helps anyone now.

steps.text: Two years later a lab publishes exactly your targeting result — without any defensive counterpart. Your buried notebook could have inoculated the public. Regrets?

choices.label: Publish the defensive work now, with the full story of why it was buried
choices.feedback: Late defense beats no defense, and the story teaches the field that burial is not a safety strategy.

choices.label: Stay buried — reopening it only draws attention
choices.feedback: The capability exists in the world without your counterweight. Silence is now complicity with the gap you left.

steps.text: The defensive paper is cited by election-integrity teams in three countries. A journalist asks: 'Did you hold back the offensive half?' How do you answer?

choices.label: Deny it — admit nothing about the withheld work
choices.feedback: The lab notebook exists; denial has a half-life. When it surfaces, the defensive work gets tainted by the lie.

choices.label: 'Yes — we published the defense and kept the targeting method restricted, and here's the review-board reasoning.'
choices.feedback: Transparent differential publication: the reasoning is public, the defense is public, the weapon isn't. That's the frontier ethos stated plainly.

simulations.debrief: Frontier capability is dual-use by default. The ethos: publish the defense, restrict the offense, document the reasoning, and never pretend burial is safety. Philosophy keeps the questions honest — including this one.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
